content: Neutral cholesterol ester hydrolase 1 (NCEH1), also referred to as arylacetamide deacetylase-like 1 (AADACL1) or KIAA1363, is an enzyme encoded by the NCEH1 gene in humans. This enzyme is localized in the endoplasmic reticulum of cells. NCEH1 catalyzes the hydrolysis of 2-acetyl monoalkylglycerol ether (2-acetyl-MAGE) as part of a biochemical pathway that regulates the levels of platelet-activating factor (PAF) and lysophospholipids. These molecules are implicated in various physiological and pathological processes, including cancer development. The enzymatic reaction facilitated by NCEH1 is as follows: 2-acetyl monoalkylglycerol ether → monoalkylglycerol ether (MAGE) Monoalkylglycerol ethers (MAGEs) can subsequently be converted into lysophospholipids, such as alkyl-lysophosphatidic acid (alkyl-LPA) and alkyl-lysophosphatidylcholine (alkyl-LPC). These lysophospholipids are bioactive lipids that play roles in cellular signaling and may contribute to oncogenic processes. Some studies have controversially suggested that NCEH1 may also hydrolyze cholesterol esters. However, experimental evidence from mouse models indicates that the loss of NCEH1 selectively reduces 2-acetyl-MAGE hydrolytic activity throughout the body, rather than affecting cholesterol ester hydrolysis. Clinical Significance NCEH1 has been implicated in cancer biology. Cancer cell lines exhibit abnormally high levels of this protein. Experimental reduction of NCEH1 expression in cancer cells leads to decreased tumor migration and growth in mouse models. Interestingly, the addition of alkyl-LPA can restore these tumor-promoting processes, suggesting a functional link between NCEH1 activity and cancer progression. NCEH1 also has the ability to degrade organophosphates, such as the pesticide metabolite chlorpyrifos oxon. Conversely, its enzymatic activity can be inhibited by organophosphates, which may have implications for toxicology and pesticide exposure. Structure NCEH1 is classified as a serine hydrolase. It contains three distinct structural domains: 1. An N-terminal transmembrane domain, which anchors the protein to cellular membranes. 2. A central catalytic domain, responsible for its enzymatic activity. 3. A lipid-binding domain located at the C-terminus, which facilitates interactions with lipid substrates. The protein exists in three isoforms, which arise from alternative mRNA splicing. These isoforms differ in their amino acid lengths: Isoform a: 448 amino acids Isoform b: 440 amino acids Isoform c: 275 amino acids
